record.paper_title: Developments and open problems on chiral polytopes
record.original_question: Determine all pairs of spherical or toroidal (d−1)-polytopes K1 and K2 such that at least one of K1 or K2 is chiral and there exists a chiral d-polytope whose facets are isomorphic to K1 and whose vertex-figures are isomorphic to K2.

evidence.quote: Problem 15 Determine all spherical or toroidal (d − 1)-polytopes K1 and K2 such that at least one of K1 or K2 is chiral and there exists a chiral d-polytope with facets isomorphic to K1 and vertex-figures isomorphic to K2.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
An abstract d-polytope is a ranked partially ordered set (with rank function taking values −1, 0, 1, …, d) satisfying the standard combinatorial axioms of abstract polytopes: it has a unique minimum face and a unique maximum face, every maximal chain (flag) has exactly d+2 elements, it is strongly flag-connected, and it satisfies the diamond condition (for any two faces F < G with rank(G) − rank(F) = 2 there are exactly two faces H with F < H < G). The facets of a d-polytope are its faces of rank d−1, and the vertex-figure at a vertex v is the section consisting of all faces strictly between v and the maximum face; both are themselves abstract (d−1)-polytopes.

An automorphism of an abstract polytope is an order-preserving bijection of its face lattice. A d-polytope P is called regular if its automorphism group acts transitively on the flags, and chiral if the automorphism group has exactly two orbits on flags such that adjacent flags lie in different orbits (so P admits all "rotational" symmetry but no reflections).

A (d−1)-polytope is called spherical if it is isomorphic to the face lattice of a convex (d−1)-polytope (equivalently, its order complex is a (d−2)-sphere), and toroidal if its underlying topological space is a (d−2)-torus (the standard locally toroidal case studied for d = 4, 5, 6).

Problem. Determine all pairs (K₁, K₂) of spherical or toroidal (d−1)-polytopes, with at least one of K₁ or K₂ being chiral, such that there exists a chiral abstract d-polytope whose facets are all isomorphic to K₁ and whose vertex-figures are all isomorphic to K₂.
artifact.status_search_result: The problem of classifying locally spherical or toroidal chiral d-polytopes with prescribed (chiral) facets and vertex-figures appears to remain open. While substantial progress has been made on the regular analogue (the classification of locally toroidal regular polytopes is complete in rank 5 and nearly complete in rank 4), and recent constructions (e.g., chiral extensions of regular toroids and chiral extensions of chiral polytopes) produce infinite families of chiral polytopes with toroidal facets, no complete classification of admissible pairs (K₁, K₂) in the chiral setting has been reported.

status_evidence.title: Chiral Extensions of Regular Toroids
status_evidence.snippet: Chiral polytopes have been built whose facets are isomorphic to a prescribed regular cubic tessellation of the n-dimensional torus; for every d≥3 there exist infinitely many chiral d-polytopes.
status_evidence.claim: Constructions yield chiral polytopes with toroidal facets, but a full classification of admissible facet/vertex-figure pairs is not claimed.

status_evidence.title: Chiral extensions of chiral polytopes
status_evidence.snippet: Constructions for chiral d-polytopes whose facets are isomorphic to a given chiral (d−1)-polytope.
status_evidence.claim: Partial existence results, not a classification.

status_evidence.title: Symmetry of Polytopes and Polyhedra (Handbook chapter)
status_evidence.snippet: Discusses the classification of locally toroidal regular polytopes (complete in rank 5, nearly complete in rank 4); chiral analogue still being developed.
status_evidence.claim: Indicates classification status is incomplete, particularly for the chiral case.
